body:
# Independent audit: distal-overlap equality and compact stability



Source: `candidate 3bb0f1835a5838c5`.

**Result: PASS in all stated dimensions and cases.** I read the complete
source and both substantive dependencies:

* `candidate cd833c78fb705a2e`;
* `candidate e2c55c91458e1e8c`.

The latter's only external geometric equality input is the ordinary
Grünbaum pyramid characterization, with its explicit apex-side orientation.
It is already separately audited in
`historical context (not an accepted premise)`. No
mixed-integer extremal classification enters this proof.

## 1. The equality chain retains actual sets

For positive a=min A_i, the distal thresholds remove exactly A_i-a from
each cap whose mass exceeds a. All hyperplane boundaries have ordinary
D-volume zero. The compact convex remainder K' therefore has volume at
least V-sum(A_i-a), and each original cap has K'-mass at most a.

Under equality in the stated overlap inequality, the lower volume bound
is a/gamma>0. The centroid of K' is contained in an original cap, giving
gamma|K'|<=a. Thus |K'|=a/gamma, K' is full-dimensional, and the removed
pieces have equality in the union bound. Integrating their indicator
excess proves pairwise zero-volume overlap; no claim of literal disjointness
at supporting boundaries is needed.

The original caps still cover every point of K'. Hence they upper-bound
its maximum ordinary depth by gamma, and Grünbaum gives the reverse bound.
The cited ordinary depth-rigidity theorem applies exactly to this
full-dimensional convex remainder and makes it a simplex.

## 2. Recovering all original halfspaces

Every original cap containing the centroid g of K' has mass exactly
gamma|K'| there. If its plane missed g strictly, translating it to g
would remove positive volume from an interior ball while preserving a
centroid cap, which is impossible. The ordinary equality characterization
then gives one of the canonical simplex vertex caps, with its correct
orientation.

Equality is in actual ambient halfspaces: a plane cutting the interior of
a full-dimensional simplex is determined by its cap trace. Every cap
missing g misses a common neighborhood after taking the minimum of the
finitely many positive distances. The caps containing g therefore cover
a neighborhood. A proper subset of the D+1 canonical cap directions
cannot do so, as the source's zero-sum barycentric perturbation shows.
Since there are precisely D+1 original caps, all must be the distinct
canonical caps. This also removes repeated caps from every equality case.

## 3. Why positive trimming is impossible for D>=2

If a removed piece has positive volume, choose a point in its intersection
with int K avoiding all other finitely many cutting planes. It belongs to
no other removed piece: otherwise the strict cap inequalities and the
interior condition give positive-volume overlap. Thus all other actual
retained inequalities are strict there. They are strict at g as well,
because g is interior to K'.

The segment to g crosses the selected cut plane inside int K with all
other inequalities still strict. A small ball at that crossing displays
a relatively open (D-1)-disk in the corresponding supporting face of K'.
This is a genuine facet. However the cap's normal is a positive multiple
of a barycentric coordinate gradient, whose maximizing support face on
the simplex K' is a singleton vertex. For D>=2 this is a contradiction.

It follows that every removed piece is empty by its definition (its
prescribed mass A_i-a is zero), no distal constraint was imposed, and
K'=K. This supplies exact body equality, not only equality of volumes.
The converse canonical simplex calculation is immediate and correct.

## 4. Positive-part equality and the one-dimensional exception

For any alpha>0, equality in the positive-part profile gives the identical
volume chain with alpha replacing a. Original caps of mass less than
alpha cannot be among all the recovered canonical caps, since each has
K'-mass alpha. The same impossible-facet argument excludes larger masses.
Thus the stronger profile statement really covers even initially
zero-mass caps, and forces all original masses to equal alpha.

The alpha>0 hypothesis is retained: at zero there are partition equality
examples which have no such simplex-cap rigidity.

The D=1 classification is also correct. Positive same-oriented interval
caps can cover only by including one full trace, giving positive overlap.
Opposite-oriented positive proper traces cover with zero overlap exactly
when they share an interior threshold. The threshold need not be the
midpoint. The higher-dimensional facet contradiction fails for precisely
the stated reason that a facet then has dimension zero.

## 5. Normalization and the attained compact modulus

A maximum-volume inscribed D-simplex exists on the compact vertex-tuple
space and has positive volume. Sending any chosen maximizing simplex to
the standard simplex T gives T subset K* and |lambda_j(x)|<=1 for every
point x of K*: replacing vertex j computes the signed volume multiplier
lambda_j(x). Hence the fixed polytope Q_D contains K*. Its coordinates
lie in [-1,1], so its Euclidean radius is at most sqrt D.

The extra condition that every inscribed simplex has volume at most
1/D! is closed under Hausdorff convergence: approximate each limiting
vertex by an actual vertex in the approximating body and pass to the
continuous determinant. The limiting bodies still contain T, so they
remain full-dimensional with a common positive volume lower bound.
The normalized body class is compact by uniformly bounded and uniformly
Lipschitz support functions.

With unit cap normals, offsets can be confined to [-R,R], R=D+1. A cap
offset below -R is replaced by -R, preserving its whole trace on every
normalized body. Positive cap masses prevent an upper offset at or above
the containing radius; no proper trace is changed by the clipping.

Under body and cap-parameter convergence, the cap indicators converge
almost everywhere outside the limiting body's boundary and finitely many
hyperplanes. These exceptional sets have zero D-volume and a common ball
dominates every integrand. Thus masses and their normalized fractions
converge. Closed coverage also persists: approximate a given limiting
body point, then select one fixed containing cap along a subsequence of
the finitely many cap indices. Passing its closed inequality to the limit
retains coverage, including all boundary points.

The conditions min A_i>=tau V and the maximal-simplex normalization
therefore define a compact covered class. A zero surplus there forces a
simplex equal to T, since it contains T and has maximal inscribed simplex
volume at most |T|. The listed canonical parameters are correct; in
particular the lambda_0 cap has unit normal -1_D/sqrt D and offset
-sqrt D/(D+1).

Hausdorff distance, normalized mass deviations, and the finite
permutation-minimized parameter discrepancy are continuous. The closed
bad set at discrepancy at least eta is compact and has no zero-surplus
point. Its positive minimum surplus is therefore attained. Taking half
that minimum gives the claimed strict discrepancy bounds even when the
hypothesis uses a non-strict surplus inequality. An empty bad set is
handled explicitly. No continuous choice of maximizing simplex is used.

## 6. Scope retained

All affine normalizations and distal cuts are operations on one ordinary
continuous body. This proof permits neither independent mixed-fiber
normalizations nor fiber-dependent distal cuts as a globally convex
mixed body. The resulting all-dimensional equality and stability laws
are legitimate inputs to a future arithmetic argument, but they do not
themselves establish the mixed-integer cap-load inequality or OC.
note: Mathematical discussion retained to expose corrections and limitations. This is not a verification run, accepted premise, or approval of the revised submission. Association follows explicit source-document references, not an inferred dependency.
